name: Kanem–Bornu Empire
summary: One of the longest-lived empires in African history, based around Lake Chad. It grew rich from trans-Saharan trade and converted to Islam in the 11th century.

location.value: Around Lake Chad: parts of Chad, Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon and Libya.

terrain.value: The Lake Chad basin, between the Sahara and the savannah.
terrain.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

climate.value: Semi-arid; Lake Chad’s size changed with the climate.
climate.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

resources.value: Salt and natron from the Lake Chad area, horses, and control of trans-Saharan trade.
resources.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

disasters.value: Droughts and the shrinking and growing of Lake Chad affected farming and grazing.
disasters.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

population.value: No reliable estimate; perhaps a few million at its height.
population.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

urbanisation.value: The capitals were Njimi in Kanem, then Ngazargamu in Bornu (from about 1470), later Kukawa.
urbanisation.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

disease.value: Unknown in detail; travellers mention fevers.
disease.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

migration.value: The court moved from Kanem to Bornu after the Bulala takeover, about 1380 in many accounts and 1390–1400 in World History Encyclopedia.
migration.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026)

economicBase.value: Trans-Saharan trade in salt, horses and slaves, plus farming and herding.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Kanem–Bornu Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

tradeRoutes.value: A trans-Saharan caravan route, in use from about 900 and running north through the Fezzan oases; goods included salt, copper, tin, cotton, hides, kola nuts, ivory, ostrich feathers, camels, gold and slaves.
tradeRoutes.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; wealth came from trade, including in enslaved people.
wealth.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

moneyAndTax.value: Cloth strips and cowries; taxes on trade.
moneyAndTax.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

inequality.value: The royal Sayfawa clan and nobles ruled over farmers, herders and slaves.
inequality.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

governmentType.value: Monarchy under the mai, with a council of nobles.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Kanem–Bornu Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (the mai and governors only)

keyRulers.value: Hu (r. 1067–1071, the first recorded Muslim ruler), Mai Dunama Dibbalemi (about 1221–1259) and Idris Alooma (late 16th century).
keyRulers.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Hu and Dunama only)

succession.value: The Duguwa dynasty was replaced by the Sayfawa in the 11th century.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Kanem–Bornu Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Sayfawa dynasty from about 1075)

institutions.value: Islamic law, a council of nobles, and officials appointed by the mai (king).
institutions.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

stability.value: One of the longest-lived empires in history.

eliteConflict.value: Civil wars between branches of the royal family in the 14th century forced a move from Kanem to Bornu.
eliteConflict.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (civil wars over succession before the Bulala takeover)

armyAndTech.value: Armoured cavalry and, under Idris Alooma, musketeers.
armyAndTech.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

majorWars.value: Long wars with the Bulala, who took Kanem between 1390 and 1400 after civil wars over succession; Idris Alooma’s campaigns (about 1564–1596).
majorWars.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Bulala only)

territoryChange.value: Expanded north and northeast under Dunama Dibbalemi (about 1221–1259) with cavalry; held the Fezzan oases from about 1300 for roughly half a century.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Kanem–Bornu Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included the Bulala, the Hausa states and later the Sokoto Caliphate.
alliancesRivals.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

inventions.value: Little is known; it imported firearms and hired Turkish musketeers under Idris Alooma.
inventions.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

scienceEducation.value: Islamic learning; Kanem scholars studied in Cairo, where a hostel was built for them.
scienceEducation.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

openness.value: Close links with North Africa and Egypt through trade and pilgrimage.
openness.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

communicationTransport.value: Trans-Saharan camel caravans; horses for cavalry; canoes on Lake Chad.

religion.value: Islam reached the rulers in the 11th century; Wikipedia names King Hummay (about 1085), while World History Encyclopedia names Hu (r. 1067–1071) as the first recorded Muslim ruler and says conversion was gradual, with widespread practice by the early 13th century.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kanem–Bornu Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026)

languageWriting.value: Kanuri was spoken; Arabic was used for writing and religion.
languageWriting.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

artsArchitecture.value: Fired-brick palaces and mosques at Ngazargamu.
artsArchitecture.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

socialStructure.value: Nobles, soldiers, scholars, farmers, herders and slaves.
socialStructure.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Islam and to the mai bound the empire together.
sharedIdentity.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

dailyLife.value: Round mud houses with thatch; brick palaces for the elite; millet, sorghum, fish and milk.

neighbours.value: The Hausa states, the Sokoto Caliphate, Bagirmi, Wadai and the Fezzan.
neighbours.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

ideasReligions.value: Helped spread Islam in the central Sahel.
ideasReligions.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

colonisation.value: Divided between Britain, France and Germany around 1900.
colonisation.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004)

riseSignals.value: Founded around 700 according to Wikipedia; World History Encyclopedia says a nomadic confederation formed probably in the 9th century, with the first written mention in 872.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kanem–Bornu Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: Kanem peaked in the late 13th century under Dunama Dibbalemi (about 1221–1259); Bornu peaked again in the late 16th century under Idris Alooma.
peakPeriod.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Kanem only)

declineSignals.value: Civil wars over succession weakened Kanem before the Bulala takeover (1390–1400); later, Fulani attacks from the Sokoto Caliphate (1808) and loss of trade.
declineSignals.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026) (civil wars and Bulala only)

outcome.value: Ended around 1900 amid colonial conquest; World History Encyclopedia says the French took it over in the late 19th century.
outcome.source: Lange, Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa (2004); World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (checked 14 Nov 2026)

sources.value: The Girgam chronicle. Checked against Wikipedia (“Kanem–Bornu Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Early history is poorly known.
